**Describe how the project/programme changes affect the investment criteria:**

*Needs of the recipient* have changed as per the investment criteria. This is relevant to all nine countries listed in the Facility, while the needs of the recipient have also changed for some of them. This has been exacerbated by the challenging global context. The COVID-19 crisis put significant pressure on city finances in these countries. Consequently, cities are facing constraints to borrow and invest in climate technologies, particularly given their initial premiums. When the pandemic first hit in 2020, many cities were already facing financial pressures due to the economic downturns in their countries. For example, in 2021, cities started to recover in 2022, but need support to ensure a green recovery as they started to face new challenges including inflation and supply chain disruptions.

### i) Strengthened delivery model and integration for integrated climate information and multi-hazard early warning systems (MHEWS) in Timor-Leste
The project will establish a national climate service (NCS) based on the GFCC to coordinate, facilitate and strengthen collaboration among national institutions for the development of an NCS. Annex B - Gender Assessment and Action Plan

1. Introduction: Relevance of Gender Mainstreaming for the Project

This Gender Assessment has been prepared as an input for the design of the Green Climate Fund (GCF) funding proposal by UN Environment Programme (UNEP), titled "Enhancing Early Warning Systems to build greater resilience to hydro-meteorological hazards in Timor-Leste". The project aims at building climate resilience and disaster preparedness capacities at national, sub-national and community level in Timor-Leste through the development of end-of-bend climate and oceans services and impact-based multi-hazard early warning systems. These systems will help communities that are most vulnerable to climate change impacts such as sea level rise, increasing mean temperatures and extreme climatic events, including droughts, floods, landslides, and cyclones.

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V2.1 | PAGE 81 OF 110

## Timor-Leste's National Adaptation Plan (NAP) (2021-2030)
As noted above, the Project is identified as a priority in the NAP and the Timor-Leste National Adaptation Strategy (NLNAS). In addition to contributing to the achievement of the following priorities and outcomes: * Strengthening the capacity of national, local institutions and communities in managing climate risks; * Reducing the vulnerability of communities to climate change impacts through increased resilience at all levels; * Enhancing institutional and community capacity to prepare for and respond to climate-induced natural disasters; * Improving disaster risk management systems and practices (including early warning); * Enhancing government and community strategies to respond to drought exacerbated by climate change; * Establishing surveillance for heat early warning systems and response mechanisms.

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V2.1 PAGE 98 OF 110

## E

This Activity will build the capacity of Timor-Leste to prepare for and respond to the impacts of climate change risks and health impacts. The Project will work with the Civil Protection Unit (CPL) - Timor- Leste, the National Directorate for Climate Change (DNCC), and the National Directorate for Disaster Management (NDM) to enhance disaster preparedness through capacity building at national level for early warning systems (EWS) and community-level for disaster risk management and co-ordination.

In addition, The Project will conduct a targeted disaster risk awareness and education campaign for women, which will focus on empowering women with the understanding and knowledge for improved disaster risk management and decision-making for climate resilience.

Annex B - Gender Assessment and Action Plan

1. Introduction: Relevance of Gender Mainstreaming for the Project

This Gender Assessment has been prepared as an input for the design of the Green Climate Fund (GCF) funding proposal by UN Environment Programme (UNEP), titled "Enhancing Early Warning Systems to build greater resilience to hydro-meteorological hazards in Timor-Leste". The project aims at building climate resilience and disaster preparedness capacities at national, sub-national and community level in Timor-Leste through the development of end-of-bend climate and oceans services and impact-based multi-hazard early warning systems. These systems will help communities that are most vulnerable to climate change impacts such as sea level rise, increasing mean temperatures and extreme climatic events, including droughts, floods, landslides, and cyclones.

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V2.1 | PAGE 18 OF 116

B

## Project Results

### i) Strengthened delivery model and integration for integrated climate information and multi-hazard early warning systems (MHEWS) in Timor-Leste
The project will establish a national climate service (NCS) based on the GFCC to coordinate, facilitate and strengthen collaboration among national institutions for the development of an NCS. The NCS will be established as a focal point for the delivery of the multi-hazard business model of the national meteorological and hydrological service (DMG). Moreover, it will instigate a best practice approach to data governance and advance the integration of climate, health, agriculture, disaster risk reduction, water and environmental management sectors in Timor-Leste.

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V2.1 PAGE 98 OF 110

## E

This Activity will build the capacity of Timor-Leste to prepare for and respond to the impacts of climate change risks and health impacts. The Project will work with the Civil Protection Unit (CPL) - Timor- Leste, the National Directorate for Climate Change (DNCC), and the National Directorate for Disaster Management (NDM) to enhance disaster preparedness through capacity building at national level for early warning systems (EWS) and community-level for disaster risk management and co-ordination.

In addition, The Project will conduct a targeted disaster risk awareness and education campaign for women, which will focus on empowering women with the understanding and knowledge for improved disaster risk management and decision-making for climate resilience.

### 4.1 - Build capacity to prepare for and respond to risks and hazards

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V2.1 | PAGE 81 OF 110

## Timor-Leste's National Adaptation Plan (NAP) (2021-2030)
As noted above, the Project is identified as a priority in the NAP and the Timor-Leste National Adaptation Strategy (NLNAS). In addition to contributing to the achievement of the following priorities and outcomes: * Strengthening the capacity of national, local institutions and communities in managing climate risks; * Reducing the vulnerability of communities to climate change impacts through increased resilience at all levels; * Enhancing institutional and community capacity to prepare for and respond to climate-induced natural disasters; * Improving disaster risk management systems and practices (including early warning); * Enhancing government and community strategies to respond to drought exacerbated by climate change; * Establishing surveillance for heat early warning systems and response mechanisms.

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND PROPOSAL V2.1 | PAGE 91 OF 110

## Result 2: Strengthened observation and monitoring, enhanced climate forecasting of critical gaps in coverage.

### Level of development of the climate information network

- Review data of the new meteorological stations
- Country inputs to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Global Observing System (GOS)
- Coordination with relevant National Project progress reports

### Timor-Leste is at a scale for climate information networks

- Supply and installation of monitoring equipment due to COVID-19 restrictions

## Result 3: Increased dissemination, sharing, communication and coordination of risk information and early warning

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V2.1 | PAGE 82 OF 116

The Project will contribute directly to Timor-Leste's achievement of progress towards these objectives.

## Engagement with civil society organisations

The Project will support an existing group of Government ministries and UN agencies responsible for coordinating disaster risk management, early warning coordination, and disaster risk reduction, expanding the group to include NGOs/CBOs and enabling the group to convey its message. The following agencies will be invited to establish a national focal point for climate services: National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA) and IOM), international NGOs (including Mercy Corps, CARE, Oxfam, PLAN, World Vision, Caritas, and others), and other relevant organisations (CIVILIS*, NHFDC**, ASHRED***, FENAMET**** and others). Existing or ad-hoc early warning related work at the community level will be leveraged to support coordination and integration into a broader national system.

plan.q: Which Green Climate Fund proposal in the corpus requested the largest amount of GCF funding (highest GCF funding requested) and what is the amount?

expect.notes: H3 corpus-wide extremum, MAX arm. DERIVATION: over all 273 registry rows, take registry.canonical(doc,'gcf_funding_requested'); keep candidates with currency=='USD' AND value is not None (the parse guard that rejects a print whose mantissa and scale word contradict each other). 172 of 273 rows qualify. The maximum is FP241 'Financing Mitigation and Adaptation Projects (FMAP) in Indian MSMEs' (Small Industries Development Bank of India, B.39 2024), raw '2149 million USD' = 2,149,000,000 USD, p.5 section A.8. Double-attested: registry.json v1 carries the same string, and the VLM extraction data/extracted/vlm/qwen_qwen2.5-vl-7b/35_gcf-b39-02-add16-rev01-funding-proposal-package-fp241.md prints '## A.8 Total GCF funding requested' / '2149 million USD (multi-country proposals: clause 19 on annex 17)'. ROBUSTNESS CHECK: FP241 is the maximum under all three defensible inclusion rules - USD any section, USD template-A.8 only, and any-currency-including-unstamped - so this expectation does not depend on which guard the concurrent extremum mechanism implements. Runner-up is FP25 at 382.5 million USD, so the winner is not close. ROWS EXCLUDED, and why: the 19 rows whose canonical value is None because the printed unit is self-contradictory - FP162 '82,849 million USD', FP53 '31,385 million USD', FP18 '$37,460 million USD', FP199 '$36,232 million USD', FP45 '34,357 | million USD', FP153 '28,654 million USD', FP68 '27 054 | million USD', FP11 '$20,546,756 million USD', FP51 'US$ 17,346 million', FP23 '9,500,000 | million USD', FP75 '$5,000,000 million USD', FP3 '7,614,280 | million USD', FP270 '50 USD', FP168 '175.9 USD', FP115 'US$ 60.0', FP114 'US$12.95', plus EUR-side FP262, FP103, FP89. Read literally, six of those would outrank FP241 (FP162 alone would read as 82.8 billion), which is exactly the trap this case exists to catch - the mechanism must exclude them, and so does this expectation. Also excluded: 21 rows priced in EUR (largest FP117, 304 million EUR - not comparable without an FX rate the corpus does not carry) and 61 rows with no gcf_funding_requested candidate at all. Denominator for an honest answer: 172 of 273 rows state a comparable USD figure. No must_not_contain: a correct answer may legitimately quote an excluded ambiguous print while explaining why it was excluded, so any forbid on those numerals would punish the honest answer. docs [] - corpus-level, answerable only from a computed note; requiring retrieval to surface FP241's package from a question that never names it would measure the wrong thing.

258. The risk assignment considers the programme’s ability to manage identified risks through mitigation measures and/or safeguards of a given risk’s impact on achievement of the intended programme results. FP270 describes implementation arrangements in which **Cambodia’s Ministry of Water Resources and Meteorology (MOWRAM) is responsible for overall project management**, with a **Project Management Unit (PMU)** that provides overall work plans and budgets, coordinates communications, coordinates with the NDCDS PIU on agriculture support activities, and implements social and environmental safeguards, among other tasks. [06_gcf-b42-02-add12-funding-proposal-package-fp270, p. 44] FP270 also states that the **PMU will be led by IFAD** and will report to the **Ministry of Economy and Finance/General Department of Resettlement (GEF-DR)** to guide the resettlement path. [06_gcf-b42-02-add12-funding-proposal-package-fp270, p. 44] It further notes that **NDCDS is responsible for implementing Component 4**, with close technical coordination between MIDWDRAM and NDCDS to ensure synergies across components. [06_gcf-b42-02-add12-funding-proposal-package-fp270, p. 44]

FP270 also describes **staffing and financial management arrangements**, stating that **MOWRAM is the lead project agency and NCCD is an implementing partner**, and that **PMU and PPU will be set up for MOWRAM and NCCD with a combined team of 10 staff members**. [06_gcf-b42-02-add12-funding-proposal-package-fp270, p. 110] The proposal says the project’s financial management and internal controls will be maintained by the **Finance Units of MOWRAM and NCCD**, supported by **contract finance staff** hired for day-to-day FM functions (e.g., maintaining records, producing reports, submitting IFR/VAT returns, and preparing budgets for IFAD). [06_gcf-b42-02-add12-funding-proposal-package-fp270, p. 110]

On **procurement implementation arrangements**, FP270 states procurement will be guided by the **IFAD Procurement Manual** and also situates procurement within Cambodia’s public procurement framework (Law on Public Procurement 2007 and related regulations/SOPs for externally financed projects). [06_gcf-b42-02-add12-funding-proposal-package-fp270, p. 108] It adds that a **Project Procurement Arrangement Letter (PALL)** will set detailed procurement requirements and thresholds, that the **NCDCDS PIU** will prepare an overall **Project Implementation Plan** and annual procurement plans aligned with the AWPBS (requiring a PID “no objection” before procurement), and that contracts will be registered and updated in IFAD’s **Contract Management Tool (CMT)** quarterly. [06_gcf-b42-02-add12-funding-proposal-package-fp270, p. 109]

As additional fiduciary/oversight measures, FP270 notes IFAD conducted financial management and procurement assessments during design and agreed additional measures to enhance executing entities’ fiduciary capacity (e.g., self-certification forms, prequalification, compliance screening of contractors/suppliers). [06_gcf-b42-02-add12-funding-proposal-package-fp270, p. 103] The retrieved excerpts do not provide the full narrative of section **B.4 “Implementation arrangements”** itself beyond the section header, so other arrangements that may be described elsewhere in that section are not visible in the excerpts surfaced here. ## C7. Institutional / Implementation Arrangements

Please describe in detail the governance structure of the project/programme, including but not limited to the principal responsible for implementation, the programme management unit, steering committee, executing entities and so on, as well as the flow of funds structures. Also describe which of these structures are already in place and which are still pending. For the pending ones, please specify the requirements to establish them.

The Director-General for Civil Protection will coordinate project implementation, with support from technical staff from all four entities supported by the project. The Administration and Accounting Unit (DAC) of the DGCP will support the project in terms of financial management and reporting as well as other administrative functions. The Project will be managed by civil servants and with support from external consultants, including for procurement and rehabilitation of hardware and infrastructure.

## Project Coordination

The NSC will be supported by two secretariat and coordination units: a project management unit with a project coordinator, financial management specialist, subproject specialist, and a monitoring and evaluation specialist; and a technical support unit.

All activities will be directly executed by the DSPC under the direct supervision from the World Bank, DNH, Mali-Meto and CEA-SAP with the support of DGPC, SAP, GFOIR, MPM, and WBG. The project management unit will provide maintenance and investment, providing staff to support project implementation, developing terms of reference and participating in the preparation of the Project Implementation Manual (PIM).

The technical support unit will provide technical assistance for project implementation and reporting. This model has been successfully tested in 2012-2015 for the implementation of the Mali EEIP and the World Bank GFOIR supported project between 2013 and 2016.

## Component 4 - Project management

This component will include support for all four entities for project coordination, monitoring and evaluation, reporting, financial management, procurement and environmental and social safeguards, technical and financial audits, development of project implementation manuals, and communication materials.
